title: Stability and Consistency Analysis of SHAP and LIME Explanations Across Machine Learning Models
venue: 2025 5th International Conference on Emerging Research in Electronics, Computer Science and Technology (ICERECT)
abstract: In the era of interpretable machine learning, explaining model predictions is essential for transparency, trust, and accountability, particularly in critical domains. This project presents a comprehensive comparative study of two widely adopted model-agnostic explanation techniques: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) and LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations). We evaluate their stability and consistency across various machine learning models, including Random Forests, Support Vector Machines, and Neural Networks, using stability metrics such as Jaccard similarity and Spearman rank correlation to assess the robustness of the top-k important features identified by each explainer under repeated sampling. Our findings reveal significant differences in the behavior of SHAP and LIME across models, indicating that SHAP generally provides more consistent and stable explanations. This study not only offers insights into the reliability of feature attributions but also aids practitioners in selecting appropriate interpretability tools based on their specific use case and model type.

title: User Centric Explainable Machine Learning for Financial Fraud Detection
venue: 2026 9th International Conference on Inventive Computation Technologies (ICICT)
abstract: The digital revolution has revolutionized the payments and financial transactions sector globally, but has also increased the reach, scale and sophistication of financial fraud. As a result, increasingly complex Automated Fraud Detection Systems have become the need of the hour for the Banking, Financial Services and Insurance (BFSI) industry today. While machine learning models are able to offer superior fraud detection prowess compared to rule-based approaches, such models often function as a black box, with little visibility into its decisions for the fraud analysts and auditors who have to deal with suspicious activity investigations. This reduces the trust and confidence in the prediction system, making it less useful in risky real-world scenarios. This paper proposes a user-centric explainable fraud transaction prediction framework. A supervised fraud transaction prediction model is built using features derived from financial transactions, and model performance is evaluated with metrics that are important for a fraud prediction use case, such as precision, recall, and F-score. The SHAP (SHapley Additive Explanations) technique is used for feature selection and post-hoc explanation of feature importance at a global level as well as for specific transactions. Further, a Natural Language layer is employed to provide human understandable summary explanations about the most important feature(s) that contributed to the decision made by the prediction model. Finally, the robustness of explanations under minor input changes is also analyzed. This framework will help provide better decision support for real-world financial fraud analysis.

title: Explainable Machine Learning for AR/VR: A Data-Driven Factor Identification Study Based on SHAP Analysis
venue: 2025 7th International Academic Exchange Conference on Science and Technology Innovation (IAECST)
abstract: This study proposes a novel explainable machine learning framework for consumer satisfaction prediction in AR/VR ecosystems by synergistically integrating Random Forest ensemble learning, Genetic Algorithm-based feature optimization, and SHAP-driven interpretability analysis. We construct a comprehensive dataset encompassing 60+ multidimensional features across hardware specifications, software ecosystems, and user interaction metrics. The hybrid predictive model achieves superior performance with RMSE of 3.625595, MAE of 2.939476, and MAPE of 4.621863%, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines including XGBoost, LightGBM, and deep learning architectures. SHAP analysis reveals demo availability, hardware specifications, and presentation strategies as primary satisfaction drivers, with significant feature interactions identified (demo-hardware synergy: 0.34; price-brand negative interaction: -0.28). Stability analysis confirms attribution robustness (Kendall's τ=0.87, p<0.001). Ablation studies validate framework reliability, and the production-ready pipeline with RESTful API deployment demonstrates practical applicability for large-scale systems.

title: Explainable AI/ML Models for Customer Retention Optimization in the Telecom Sector
venue: 2025 IEEE 1st International Conference on Recent Trends in Computing and Smart Mobility (RCSM)
abstract: Customer churn remains one of the costliest operational problems for telecommunications providers. Predictive models that detect at-risk customers can materially reduce churn, but black-box algorithms hinder operational adoption because product teams, regulators and customer-facing staff need understandable reasons for automated recommendations. This paper presents an end-to-end, explainable machine learning pipeline for customer retention optimization that combines tabular usage/billing features with short support-call text, evaluates interpretable and high-performance learners (logistic regression, Random Forest, XGBoost), and applies both local (LIME) and global (SHAP/feature importance) explainers. We propose reproducible preprocessing, stratified cross-validation, and stability measures for explanations, and we show how explanations feed a policy simulator that converts predictions into intervention decisions (discounts, proactive calls, tailored bundles). Using a mixed tabular + text telecom dataset, the pipeline demonstrates strong discrimination (AUC) for ensemble models while retaining actionable local explanations for top-risk cases. We report mock quantitative results and human evaluation metrics (actionability, trust, explanation consistency) to illustrate typical outcomes and trade-offs. Finally, we discuss operational integration, ethical safeguards, and deployment recommendations for a hybrid scoring+ explainability architecture. Implementation details and methodology choices follow established enterprise XAI practices and the uploaded methodological reference.

title: Towards More Stable LIME For Explainable AI
venue: 2022 International Symposium on Intelligent Signal Processing and Communication Systems (ISPACS)
abstract: Although AI's development is remarkable, end users do not know how the AI has come to a specific conclusion due to the black-box nature of AI algorithms like deep learning. This has given rise to the field of explainable AI (XAI) where techniques are being developed to explain AI algorithms. One such technique is called Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME). LIME is popular because it is modelagnostic and works well with text, tabular and image data. While it has some good features, there are still room for improvements towards the original LIME algorithm especially it's stability. In this work, the LIME stability is being reviewed and three different approaches were investigated for its effectiveness in stability improvement which are; 1) using high sample size for stable ordering, 2) using an averaging method to reduce region flipping; and 3) to evaluate different super-pixels segmentation algorithms in generating stable LIME outcome. The experiment results shows a definite increase in the stability of the improved LIME compared to the baseline LIME and thus the reliability of using it practically.

title: Enhancing Intrusion Detection Reliability Through Explainable Machine Learning Models
venue: 2026 IEEE Global Symposium on Emerging and Communication Technologies (GSEACT)
abstract: Network attack detection is difficult in the age of Artificial Intelligence. Intrusion detection need AI-based method to detect attacks over the network. But all methods are behaving like a black box model. This paper presents an explainable intrusion detection framework with integrates machine learning classifiers. This paper used CIC2018 dataset for processing. This network traffic data is preprocessed using normalization and dimensionality reduction. Support Vector Machine, Decision Tree, Random Forest, and Naïve Bayes classifiers are trained to detect malicious activity. This paper explore this black box result of machine learning methods using explainable AI. In addition to conventional performance metrics, explanation stability is evaluated to assess consistency of model reasoning across experiments. Local explanation analysis i.e Local Interpretable Modelagnostic Explanations (LIME) is applied to identify features for individual predictions. Experimental results demonstrate that ensemble learning achieves strong detection performance. It also maintaining reliable interpretability, making the framework suitable for security-critical environments.

title: Leakage-Safe and Explainable Tree-Ensemble Benchmark for GDSC Drug Sensitivity (ln(IC50)) Prediction
venue: 2026 IEEE 2nd International Conference on Quantum Photonics, Artificial Intelligence & Networking (QPAIN)
abstract: This paper has a reproducible, leakage-safe benchmarking of predicting cancer drug sensitivity (ln(IC50)) on the GDSC dataset using tabular regression models. Our findings are reported when under a strict hold-out protocol with an untouched test set, and we also test group-based generalization conditions (cold-cell-line splits, per-drug splits) to minimize optimism due to row-wise splits. Ensuring good bases are tree ensembles (ExtraTrees and Random Forest) and we also add modern tabular deep learning baselines under the same leakage insensitive preprocessing. Lastly, we supplement predictive accuracy with analyses of the explanations and quantify the stability of explanations by using bootstrap and input-perturbation tests.

title: From Symptoms to Clinical Insight: An Explainable Machine Learning Framework for Early Diabetes Screening
venue: 2026 IEEE 2nd International Conference on Quantum Photonics, Artificial Intelligence & Networking (QPAIN)
abstract: Early diabetes screening based on symptoms is especially useful in conditions of resource shortage where access to laboratory tests is limited. Yet, most previous work tends to center around one specific top-performing model and does not explore whether model interpretability is maintained under diverse learning paradigms. In this work, we present a multi-model explainable machine learning framework with a focus on robustness and explanation stability for symptom-based screening. Employing the UCI Sylhet Early-Stage Diabetes dataset ($\text{5 2 0}$ instances, 17 categorical attributes), eight classifiers are evaluated through stratified train-test splitting, cross-validation, and overfitting analysis. Bootstrap resampling is used to derive confidence intervals for performance estimates. Finally, beyond performance, we study the reliability of explanations: SHAP-based global attributions are computed for heterogeneous models (RF, SVM-RBF, and MLP), with local interpretability demonstrated using SHAP and LIME. Then, we introduce an Explainability Stability Score $S(j) \in[0], [1]$, which quantifies cross-model consensus on symptom importance. We find that symptoms such as polyuria and polydipsia are consistently dominant across architectures, though several features displaying model-specific importance. This stability-driven symptom hierarchy provides a clinically interpretable ranking of indicators and enables clinicians or community health workers to prioritize a reduced and reliable subset of symptoms for transparent early-stage screening, particularly in resource-constrained and LMIC settings.

title: Adversarial Robustness and Explainability in Intrusion Detection Systems: Maintaining XAI Integrity Under Adversarial Attacks
venue: 2026 International Conference on Air Defense and Security (ICADS)
abstract: Military networks are susceptible to cyber attacks. Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) are developing to defend military assets using machine learning models combined with explainable techniques, such as SHAP, allowing military operators to have high accuracy when detecting intrusions, yet also be able to understand how decisions are made. However, there still remains the critical area of researching the interactions between adversarial attacks and explainability for IDSs. This paper tries to fill this gap by looking into the interactions between adversarial attacks and explainable AI (XAI) in terms of network intrusion detection. Our research demonstrates that existing IDS models have moderate accuracy (70.6% classifying a FGSM attack, and 70.8% classifying a PGD attack), however, the SHAP explanations for the model become less accurate during adversarial attacks. Therefore, the operators may not trust the accuracy of the IDS model's output due to less accurate model explanations. We propose an adversarial training method that improves the overall robustness of the model (80.6% classifying a FGSM attack, and 80.4% classifying a PGD attack) while maintaining reliable SHAP explanations. Additionally, our results indicate that XAI explanation stability can be preserved during adversarial training, which creates an opportunity to close a major research gap in the fields of robustness and interpretability. Thus, this study will enable military operators to be confident in making AI-driven support decisions during military operations where military operations require both high accuracy and high transparency in their decision-making.

title: XAI for Generalizable Intrusion Detection: Cross-Dataset Feature Attribution with Real-Time Alert Integration
venue: 2026 IEEE Global Symposium on Emerging and Communication Technologies (GSEACT)
abstract: Cyber threat detection has advanced with the integration of machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) in intrusion detection systems (IDS). However, the black-box nature of these models limits their adoption in mission-critical environments. This paper presents an explainable IDS framework that combines local and global interpretability through SHAP and LIME. We evaluate six ML/DL models on two widely used datasets, CICIDS2017 and SIMARGL2022, and perform a cross-dataset interpretability analysis to examine whether feature attributions remain consistent for semantically similar traffic classes. This form of interpretability-level generalization is a rarely addressed but essential dimension of model trustworthiness. We also implement a novel real-time alerting mechanism via WhatsApp (using the Twilio API), allowing human analysts to receive interpretable alerts instantly. Explainability is then measured by six XAI metrics, such as fidelity and stability. Results indicate that the system presented here has high predictive accuracy while improving transparency, robustness, and real-world usability, filling the gap between automated detection and human-centric security operations. In addition, we assess explanation robustness using SHAP stability analysis under input perturbations, highlighting the reliability of explanations in noisy environments. We propose RANK-ECI, a stability metric based on Kendall's Tau, to measure explanation consistency under input perturbations.

title: Explaining the Black Box: An XAI-Driven Trustworthiness Audit of ML-Based IoT Intrusion Detection Across Attack Categories
abstract: Machine learning classifiers for Internet of Things (IoT) intrusion detection routinely report accuracy above 99%, yet this conceals systematic failures on operationally important minority categories such as BruteForce and Web-based attacks, and the global explainability analyses usually applied to these models say nothing about how their decision logic varies from one threat type to another. We argue that a third property matters alongside detection and explanation: whether a classifier explains different attacks in a consistent way. To measure it, we introduce the Explanation Consistency Score (ECS), a model-agnostic metric based on the Jaccard similarity of top-K SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) feature sets. To the best of our knowledge, no directly equivalent measure was identified in the literature reviewed here for cross-category explanation consistency in multiclass intrusion detection. Applying ECS in a per-category audit of four classifiers (Decision Tree, Random Forest, XGBoost, and Logistic Regression) on CICIoT2023, we find that performance and explanation consistency pull against one another. XGBoost is the strongest detector (Macro-F $1=0.883$ , Balanced Accuracy = 0.847), with near-perfect recall on Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS), Denial of Service (DoS), and Mirai but F1 of only 0.708 and 0.706 on BruteForce and Web-based attacks, and among the tree-based models it records the lowest ECS, 0.396 at K = 10, against 0.521 for Decision Tree. Logistic Regression records a lower ECS still, 0.291, but performs poorly on detection and so falls outside the pattern. A within-model correlation between ECS and per-category F1 is reported for completeness in Section V-H, but with only seven categories it is underpowered and we do not draw conclusions from it. We treat this trade-off as an empirical model-selection characteristic to be audited, not a defect to be removed.

title: Auditable Credit Scoring: Explainable Models with Stable Rationales on Tabular Data
venue: 2026 International Conference on AI-Driven Smart Systems and Ubiquitous Computing (ICAUC)
abstract: Credit decisioning systems must balance strong predictive performance with transparency and accountability to satisfy regulatory and ethical requirements. This paper presents a practical explainable AI framework that integrates accurate modeling with interpretable, post hoc explanations and systematic diagnostic analysis. Rather than relying solely on traditional accuracy based evaluation, the framework assesses model calibration, explanation stability, and the influence of sensitive or proxy attributes revealed through interpretability techniques. We evaluate the approach using five widely studied credit datasets: Adult Census Income, German Credit, Taiwan Credit Default, LendingClub FICO, and HMDA. Experimental results show that ensemble and deep learning models achieve competitive predictive performance while explanation methods such as SHAP and LIME provide coherent and consistent global and local insights into model behavior. Well performing models demonstrate stable reliance on financially meaningful features, whereas weaker models exhibit inconsistent explanatory patterns. Importantly, interpretability based analyses uncover potential fairness risks that are not apparent from predictive metrics alone, underscoring the diagnostic value of explanations in regulated decision making contexts. To support transparency and independent auditing, we release complete implementation artifacts to enable reproducibility. The findings demonstrate that combining calibrated predictions with stable, interpretable explanations is both feasible and essential for trustworthy credit decisioning..

title: A Novel Stability Control Method for Hybrid AC/DC Power Grid Based on SHAP-LightGBM
venue: 2025 5th IEEE International Conference on Energy Engineering and Power Systems (EEPS)
abstract: This paper proposes an efficient and reliable stability control method for AC/DC hybrid grids based on a combination of SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and the Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) model. The shortcomings of traditional stability control approaches are adressed, which are often slow and heavily reliant on expert experience. Then by leveraging the predictive power of a pretrained LightGBM model, the system can rapidly assess the stability status of the power grid after a fault occuring. If instability is detected, SHAP is employed to interpret the model's prediction and quantify the contribution of each generator's power output to the instability. The targeted and prioritized adjustment of generator outputs to restore system stability quickly and accurately is allowed. The proposed method can significantly enhance the safety and reliability of power systems, providing a rapid and effective response mechanism for post-fault recovery in complex AC/DC hybrid grids.

title: Explainable Machine Learning for Effective Malware Detection in Encrypted Network Traffic
venue: 2026 IEEE Ural-Siberian Conference on Biomedical Engineering, Radioelectronics and Information Technology (USBEREIT)
abstract: Transport Layer Security is the backbone of secure web communication today. It was designed to provide confidentiality, integrity, and authentication on untrusted networks, such as the Internet. With encryption becoming an essential component in protecting the integrity and confidentiality of data, it simultaneously makes the process of intrusion detection more difficult. Although machine learning approaches have demonstrated impressive accuracy in detecting malicious encrypted traffic using flow-level metadata, their black-box nature restricts operational trust and seamless integration into Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response environments. In this work, an explainable machine learning framework for the detection of malicious encrypted traffic is proposed using metadata-derived flow statistics and temporal patterns. We employ multiple featureselection strategies, including Analysis of Variance statistical filtering and Shapley Additive Explanation importance ranking, on tree-based models to investigate the trade-off between detection performance and interpretability. The experimental results show that feature reduction supported by statistical validations not only preserves competitive accuracy but also improves explanation consistency and operational efficiency. The paper concludes by exploring how explainability improves trust in security automation workflows by translating model decisions into clear and actionable insights.

title: XAI-Informed Iterative Development (XIID): An Architecture to Construct High-Performance, Explainable Loan Default Prediction Models
venue: 2026 IEEE 6th International Conference on Smart Information Systems and Technologies (SIST)
abstract: The black-box opaqueness of a machine learning model is a critical limitation to the superiority of machine learning in loan default prediction. Although Explainable AI (XAI) methods such as SHAP are frequently used after-hoc to produce an explanation, they are not linked to the model development cycle, and sometimes it is a simple rationalization of decisions based on the volatile patterns. The paper suggests the innovation of the XAIInformed Iterative Development (XIID) framework which actively addresses the concept of explainability into the pipeline of modelingly development. XIAI diagnostics within XIID (the analysis of SHAP interaction values, local explanation stability, consistency of feature contribution) are systematic to find the gaps in the model. Feature engineering, data quality interventions and model architecture refinements are the lessons to focus in a closed loop. Trained on three datasets of publicly lending data (LendingClub, GiveMeSomeCredit, German Credit) with LightGBM, models developed by XIID shows statistically significant higher performance than standard post-hoc explained control models: average AUC gain of 2.3 % ($\mathbf{p}<0.05$) and at the same time generate explanations with $\mathbf{2 1. 5 \%}$ higher fidelity (AOPC) and $\mathbf{2 6. 8 \%}$ more stability (Jaccard similarity). The model fills the much-needed gap of performance and interpretability, and offers a systematically structured approach to the development of credit risk systems that are precise, transparent, auditable, and trustworthy to regulatory compliance.

title: Explainable Machine Learning Framework for Phishing URL Detection with a Realistic Large-Scale Dataset
venue: 2026 8th International Congress on Human-Computer Interaction, Optimization and Robotic Applications (ICHORA)
abstract: Phishing attacks remain a major cybersecurity threat, often evading traditional blacklist-based defenses through continuously evolving URLs. While machine learning (ML) methods achieve high detection performance, their lack of interpretability limits practical adoption. This study proposes an explainable phishing URL detection framework supported by a newly constructed large-scale dataset of 579,920 URLs. Unlike conventional domain-based collections, realistic and structurally diverse legitimate URLs are generated using protocol variations and a two-stage web crawling strategy, reducing dataset bias and improving generalization. Six ML models and three ensemble strategies are evaluated, where LightGBM achieves the best base performance and stacking ensembles provide marginal gains. For interpretability, global explanations are obtained using SHAP and permutation importance, while local decisions are analyzed with SHAP and LIME. Additionally, a SHAP stability analysis based on Spearman correlation demonstrates highly consistent feature importance rankings across different sample sizes. The results show that the proposed framework enables accurate, robust, and reliable explainable phishing detection for real-world applications.

title: Towards Quality Measures for xAI algorithms: Explanation Stability
venue: 2023 IEEE 10th International Conference on Data Science and Advanced Analytics (DSAA)
abstract: The domain of Artificial Intelligence has become ubiquitous across a wide plethora of domains and is now an integral part of the daily life of the ordinary citizen. While the need for increased transparency of the highly accurate black-box model is an important and very active area of research, the produced explanations themselves might not always be accurate. The measures to assess the quality of explanations are an important research topic. In this paper, a set of extensive experiments is performed to evaluate the stability of SHAP explanations under conditions of different noise types and different noise intensities as an effort to build a formal way of assessing the quality of explanations provided by the SHAP algorithm. The experiments are performed on four different datasets, with three different noise types at four different strength levels. The impact of the scenarios on SHAP explanations is reported, the implications for the evaluation of explainability methods are elaborated upon, along with the significance of the results for the SHAP method of explanations. The future directions are laid out thereafter.

title: Cross-Model Analysis of Token-Level Explanations in Tatar Text Classification
venue: 2026 IEEE Ural-Siberian Conference on Biomedical Engineering, Radioelectronics and Information Technology (USBEREIT)
abstract: The aim of this work is to evaluate the performance, interpretability, and consistency of explanations generated by different Explainable AI (XAI) methods for different machine learning models trained on a Tatar language text classification task. Explanations were generated by using Integrated Gradients and LIME methods, and aggregated to obtain global importance scores. Inter-model similarity of explanations was assessed by using Spearman rank correlation and Jaccard overlap, while cross-model consensus was identified through bootstrap confidence intervals and Kendall’s coefficient of concordance. Although classifiers demonstrated comparable predictive performance, their global explanatory patterns differed substantially. But a subset of architectureindependent tokens showed statistically stable and directionally consistent influence across models. The proposed framework enables systematic evaluation of explanation stability and is applicable to low-resource NLP languages requiring transparent and robust model analysis. The work contributes both to the field of computational linguistics for Turkic languages and to the methodology of interpreting different machine learning models for text data.

title: Can We Explain What We Anonymize? On the Impact of Data Anonymization on Post-hoc Model Explanations
venue: 2026 IEEE European Symposium on Security and Privacy Workshops (EuroS&PW)
abstract: Privacy-preserving data publishing and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) are both essential for trustworthy machine learning, yet their interaction remains largely underexplored. In practice, models are often trained on anonymized datasets, but little is known about how classical anonymization techniques affect post-hoc explanations. In this paper, we provide a systematic empirical study of how feature attribution rankings change under widely used anonymization models, including k-anonymity, $\ell$-diversity, t closeness, and $(\alpha, k)$-anonymity. Across multiple real-world datasets and classifiers, we compare explanations generated by SHAP and LIME and quantify their stability using rank correlation and hypothesis testing. Our findings reveal a fundamental trade-off: explainable privacy-preserving models are feasible under mild privacy constraints, but strict anonymization requirements often lead to unstable explanations and severe utility degradation.

title: Hybrid AI for Predictive Cyber Risk Assessment: Federated Graph-Transformer Architecture With Explainability
abstract: The increasing complexity and dynamism of modern digital infrastructures have significantly elevated the difficulty of anticipating and mitigating cyber threats. Traditional risk assessment methods, often based on static rules and signature matching, fail to provide sufficient predictive capabilities in scenarios characterized by high-volume, heterogeneous data and evolving attack patterns. Furthermore, conventional machine learning models lack architectural flexibility and contextual awareness to detect stealthy or multi-stage attacks across distributed environments. This paper proposes a hybrid model for predictive cyber risk assessment that integrates Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for relational pattern modeling, a Transformer-based language model (CyberBERT) for semantic representation of logs and traffic data, and a Federated Learning framework to preserve data privacy during training. The model was trained and evaluated using public datasets (CIC-IDS2017, UNSW-NB15, MITRE ATT&CK, TON_IoT) and synthetically generated traffic from honeypots and real anonymized networks. The system achieved an average F1-score of 0.947, significantly outperforming traditional classifiers such as SVM (0.836), Random Forest (0.873), and standard deep neural networks (0.901). Including adversarial training improved attack detection by 21.3 % under evasion scenarios. Furthermore, the model supports interpretability through SHAP and LIME, reaching an 83.5 % concordance in explanation consistency. The architecture demonstrates scalability and low-latency inference on edge and cloud platforms, making it suitable for real-time deployment in heterogeneous environments. These results highlight the model’s capability to deliver accurate, resilient, and privacy-preserving predictions of cyber risks across dynamic and distributed infrastructures.

title: Explainable and Trust-Oriented Evaluation for Determining Suitable Augmented and Synthetic Data Proportions in IoT Intrusion Detection
venue: IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems
abstract: Artificial-data inclusion can improve IoT intrusion detection, but predictive performance alone cannot establish the trustworthiness of the model. This study presents an explainable and trust-oriented evaluation for determining suitable proportions of augmented and synthetic data in IoT intrusion-detection training. Experiments are conducted on the UM-NIDS and CICIoT datasets using original-data b...

title: MLAllergen: Predicting Allergenicity Using Peptide Structural and Physicochemical Features
venue: 2025 International Conference on Informatics, Multimedia, Cyber and Information System (ICIMCIS)
abstract: The increasing global prevalence of food and environmental allergies has necessitated the development of efficient methods for allergen prediction. In response, MLAllergen, a computational framework, was introduced to predict allergenicity using machine learning by leveraging structural and physicochemical properties of peptides. A total of 36 key descriptors—including charge, isoelectric point, and instability index—were extracted from curated datasets comprising 2,391 allergenic and 2,363 non-allergenic proteins. Five supervised models (XGBoost, LightGBM, Random Forest, SVC, and Logistic Regression) were evaluated. Among five evaluated models, superior performance was achieved by LightGBM (accuracy: 0.9487, AUC: 0.9904), followed closely by XGBoost (accuracy: 0.9424, AUC: 0.9863). Through SHAP analysis, electrostatic properties (charge, charge density) and stability indices were identified as key discriminators, consistent with known immunological mechanisms. In contrast to sequence-based NLP approaches, the physicochemical feature-based method employed here provided enhanced interpretability and performance. These findings indicate that the machine learning models achieved strong predictive performance; however, the underlying physicochemical descriptor-based approach could also be effectively applied to deep learning (DL) frameworks. The integration of physicochemical descriptors with deep learning–based feature extraction capabilities may further enhance allergen prediction accuracy. The critical role of protein biophysics in immune recognition has been underscored, positioning MLAllergen as a robust and extensible computational tool for advancing allergen prediction and research in computational allergology.

title: Novel Explainable CNN-LightGBM Model for Smartphone Continuous Authentication
abstract: Smartphones have become integral to our everyday activities, from storing significant amounts of private information to serving as access points to various online services. However, one-time authentication techniques such as Personal Identification Number (PIN) and passwords are no longer sufficient to keep our data secure as they do not ensure user identity verification after the initial login. Beyond these traditional methods, numerous robust authentication techniques have been developed for smartphones, including behavioral biometrics such as gait analysis, keystroke dynamics, and touch-gesture recognition, as well as physiological biometrics including fingerprint, facial recognition, and voice authentication. Despite their promise, these existing techniques still exhibit notable research gaps, including limited classification accuracy and high Equal Error Rates. Furthermore, most existing continuous authentication systems lack transparency in their decision-making processes, failing to incorporate explainability mechanisms. This paper proposes a novel, explainable device-level continuous authentication system for smartphones that combines a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) with a Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM). The system continuously verifies user identity by analyzing behavioral patterns captured through built-in smartphone sensors. Using the ExtraSensory dataset, our model achieves an average accuracy of 98.7% and an average Equal Error Rate (EER) of 2.07%. This performance is competitive with or surpasses that of other state-of-the-art systems, including Adaptive Recurrent Neural Network (Adaptive-RNN), Polynomial Neural Networks and deep neural network-based approaches, under similar evaluation protocols. Additionally, to address the critical challenge of explainability in continuous authentication, the Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) technique has been incorporated, ensuring transparency in the model’s decision-making process through multiple instances of both legitimate and imposter classes. We additionally validate our findings using SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) to ensure robustness of explanations.

title: Evaluating Ensemble Learning and Explainability Consistency for Multi-Class Osteosarcoma Classification
venue: 2026 IEEE 2nd International Conference on Quantum Photonics, Artificial Intelligence & Networking (QPAIN)
abstract: Osteosarcoma is an aggressive bone malignancy, predominantly affecting children and young adults. Its subtypes must be identified early and accurately to inform better treatment planning and improve patient outcomes. In this Study, we investigate the performance and interpretability of ensemble learning models for multi-class osteosarcoma detection using texture-based radiomic features. We have evaluated five baseline machine learning models and fifteen ensemble models, including bagging, boosting, voting, and stacking, under a unified preprocessing pipeline that incorporates SMOTE, feature scaling, and hyperparameter optimization. The results demonstrates that ensemble methods (soft voting and tuned stacking) outperform individual classifiers, achieving an F1-score of up to 0.8665. This work also presents a Dual-XAI agreement framework to analyze the reliability of explanations. After analyzing the SHAP and Permutation Importance individually and in agreement, there is moderate discrepancy on the explanation SHAP and Permutation Importance explained. Permutation Importance also indicated there is high overlap of the influential features but the variable features from high to low position on the list of data partitions. This suggests explanation algorithms that predict with SHAP and Permutation Importance on the same data sets do not stable explanations. This work suggests that the primary focus of the framework is to evaluate performance and analyze individual and joint explainability of stability, reliability, and transparency of a given predictive model so that it is safe to deploy predictive models of ensemble learning in a clinical decision support system.

title: Validity of Feature Importance in Low-Performing Machine Learning for Tabular Biomedical Data
abstract: In tabular data analysis, high model accuracy is often regarded as a prerequisite for discussing feature importance. This assumption stems from the expectation that the validity of feature importance correlates with model performance. In this work, we challenge this prevailing belief by demonstrating that even low-performing models can provide reliable feature importance on biomedical datasets. We conduct experiments to observe how feature importance rankings change as model performance progressively degrades. Using three synthetic datasets and four real-world biomedical datasets, we compare feature rankings from the full datasets to those obtained after reducing either the number of samples (samples removal) or the number of features (features removal), using different feature stability indices. Our results reveal that, in both synthetic and real datasets, feature rankings remain stable during performance degradation caused by features removal. In contrast, sample removal introduces greater discrepancies in feature importance rankings as performance deteriorates more severely. By analyzing the distribution of feature importance values and theoretically examining the probability that the model fails to distinguish importance between features, we show that models can still reliably identify feature importance despite performance degradation due to features removal. We conclude that the validity of feature importance can be preserved even at suboptimal model performance levels, as long as the degradation stems from insufficient features rather than insufficient samples. This has a considerable impact on biomedical research, where feature importance analysis plays a pivotal role in clinical decision support and translational bioinformatics.

title: Exploring Ranked Local Selectors for Stable Explanations of ML Models
venue: 2021 Second International Conference on Intelligent Data Science Technologies and Applications (IDSTA)
abstract: While complex machine learning methods can achieve great performance, human-interpretable details of their internal reasoning is to a large extent unavailable. Interpretable machine learning can remedy the lack of access to model reasoning but remains an elusive feat to fully achieve. Here we propose ranked selectors as a method for post-hoc explainability of classification outcomes from arbitrary classification models, with an initial emphasis on tabular data of moderate dimensions. The method is based on constructing a set of selectors, or rules, delimiting a local class consistent domain with maximal cover around the item of interest. The extended adjacent feature space is probed to achieve a ranking of the selectors. The method supports the use of an explicit foil class Q, allowing the formulation of contrastive queries in the form “Why inference P instead of alternative inference Q?”. The answer is given as a short list of disjoint rules, a format previously shown to be amenable to human interpretation. We demonstrate the proposed method in open datasets, and elaborate on its stability aspects relative to other comparable methods.

title: Explanation-Stable Anomaly Detection for Imbalanced Heterogeneous Tabular Data Under Distribution Shift
venue: 2026 5th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Internet of Things and Cloud Computing Technology (AIoTC)
abstract: Anomaly detection in heterogeneous tabular data is critical for applications such as insurance risk analytics, transportation safety, financial fraud detection, network intrusion monitoring, and predictive maintenance. These domains often rely on large-scale structured datasets in which rare but consequential events must be identified under evolving real-world conditions. Real-world deployments face three co-occurring challenges: extreme class imbalance where anomalies constitute less than one percent of observations, distribution shift between training and deployment environments, and the need for consistent post-hoc explanations to support human decision-making, particularly in safety-critical and risk-sensitive settings. Existing methods typically address these issues in isolation. We propose ShiftX-TabAD, a unified framework built upon the FT-Transformer backbone that jointly tackles all three challenges. ShiftX-TabAD integrates three complementary modules: (i) imbalance-aware representation learning via supervised contrastive loss with class-balanced sampling, (ii) distribution-shift-aware sample reweighting using density ratio estimation, and (iii) explanation-stability regularization that constrains gradient-based feature attributions to remain consistent across shifted domains. Experiments on five public tabular anomaly detection benchmarks under a synthetic shift protocol demonstrate that ShiftX-TabAD improves AUC-PR by an average of 8.4 percentage points over the strongest baseline under the 0.5% anomaly-ratio setting, while reducing attribution drift scores by 56-59% relative to the best competing method. These results suggest that incorporating explanation stability as a training objective can improve both the robustness and explanation consistency of tabular anomaly detectors.

title: Explainable Inverse NaïVe Bayes (EINB): A Fast and Trustworthy Approach to Explainability Based on Inverse Probability Inference
venue: 2025 IEEE/WIC International Conference on Web Intelligence and Intelligent Agent Technology (WI-IAT)
abstract: Despite the high performance of black-box approaches, such as deep learning, their opaque decision-making raises concerns regarding their social implementation. Existing representative explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods, such as local interpretable model-agnostic explanations (LIME) and Shapley additive explanations (SHAP), offer model-agnostic explanations but rely on input perturbations (noise), leading to high computational costs and explanation instability. This study presents explainable inverse Naïve Bayes (EINB), a novel approach grounded in inverse probability inference from Bayes' theorem. EINB uses the internal likelihood distributions of the Naïve Bayes classifier to analytically derive global feature importance using the Kullback-Leibler divergence between class distributions and local prediction contribution using the log-likelihood ratio between classes without requiring input perturbations. Qualitative and quantitative evaluations using the Titanic and Breast Cancer datasets confirmed that EINB can generate explanations consistent with human intuition. Compared with LIME and SHAP, EINB achieved up to 115 times higher computational efficiency and three times higher explanation conciseness without compromising explanation fidelity while maintaining complete robustness against input perturbations. These results demonstrate that the proposed approach, which uses a model's internal generative knowledge and directly evaluates the “evidence weight” of each class based on the observed data, is highly effective in addressing the limitations of existing methods while achieving fast and highly reliable explainability. The findings of this study offer an effective alternative to current XAI methods, reinforce the importance of “designing interpretable models,” and contribute to trustworthy AI system development.

title: Quantifying the Consistency of Explainable Cardiovascular Screening through Multi Metric Stability Auditing of Population Scale Models
venue: 2026 1st International Conference on Innovation & Growth in Next-Gen Intelligent Technology & Engineering (IGNITE)
abstract: The scalable cardiovascular risk prediction framework was constructed to assess the consistency and reliability of model elucidations in comparison to scale of datasets. The research was a comparison of a baseline model which was trained on the UCI Cleveland dataset and an ensemble-based model which is XGBoost with training on a 70,000 record cardiovascular dataset. Explainability stability was evaluated with the help of a structured Stress Test based on randomized cross-validation and measures, such as Spearman Ranking Consistency, Jaccard Feature Overlap, and Explainer Consensus across SHAP and LIME. It was found that there was a significant Stability Gap between small-sample and population-scale modeling. The model based in Cleveland had moderate stability with feature ranking correlation approximately 0.80 and 40 percent primary feature agreement indicating that attribution behavior is not reliable. Comparatively, the population-scale solution obtained almost perfect ranking consistency (ρ≈0.99) and full primary driver alignment. This supports the conclusion that data scale is a stabilizing influence and the view that stability auditing should be mandated prior to clinical implementation of machine learning-based decision support systems.

title: Interpretability vs Accuracy: Stability Using SHAP Explanations Under Noisy Training Data
venue: 2026 1st International Conference on AI, Data Science, Cyber Security and Smart Manufacturing for Sustainable Development (ICADCS)
abstract: Machine learning models are becoming to be used more and more in high-stakes domains such as healthcare. These domains wants predictive model performance to be accurate but also the interpretability is required to be reliable. Although there has been substantial literature work done to be investigate the robustness of predictive accuracy under degraded data quality, but stability of model explanation has received comparatively limited attention. This study systematically studies the impact or effects of controlled data quality degradation in both predictive performance and interpretability stability using the Cleveland Heart Disease dataset. Gaussian noise has been gradually injected into training data to simulate realistic measurement imperfections observed in real world scenarios. As the baseline classifier, the Logistic regression model is trained and feature importance is determined using SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values. Interpretability is assessed using the feature importance ranking consistency under each noise levels. While the results show that predictive accuracy will drop very slowly, interpretability stability will be lost much faster. Therefore, the authors propose that the robustness of explanations is one of the characteristics of trustworthy AI which cannot simply be derived from the performance metrics of prediction.

title: Explanation Consistency as a Trust Signal in Human–AI Teaming
venue: 2026 IEEE International Conference on Omni Layer Intelligent Systems (COINS)
abstract: Post-hoc explanation methods such as SHAP and LIME are widely used in human-AI decision support, yet they can produce inconsistent explanations for the same prediction under minor perturbations, changes in background samples, or different random seeds. This instability raises concerns about whether explanations provide a reliable basis for user trust and reliance. We introduce a framework for quantifying and reducing explanation inconsistency in tabular decision-support settings. First, we propose a distributional consistency metric based on Jensen–Shannon distance that measures agreement across repeated explanation runs and explanation methods. Second, we introduce Explanation Stability Regularization (ESR), a consistency-aware regularization and model-selection approach that penalizes attribution variability while monitoring predictive performance. Finally, we evaluate the relationship between explanation consistency and human-AI teaming outcomes through a controlled study using tabular classification tasks from the UCI Adult Income and COMPAS datasets. Across three model classes, ESR improves explanation consistency while maintaining comparable predictive accuracy in the tabular settings studied here. Participants exposed to more consistent explanations report higher trust, make more accurate decisions, and show better-calibrated reliance in the controlled study. These findings suggest that explanation consistency can serve as a useful trust signal for tabular human-AI decision support, while broader generalization to expert users, high-stakes settings, and higher-dimensional domains remains an important direction for future work.

title: The Rigidity Paradox: Decoupled Drift and Attribution in Cross-Domain Clinical ML Monitoring
venue: 2026 6th International Conference on Emerging Smart Technologies and Applications (eSmarTA)
abstract: This paper investigates a critical failure mode in cross-domain clinical machine learning, termed the Rigidity Paradox, where model predictions degrade under distributional shift while feature attributions remain relatively unchanged. An XGBoost model trained on the Cleveland cohort was evaluated across geographically distinct populations (Hungary, Switzerland, and VA Long Beach) under a strict domain-separation protocol. Despite a notable performance drop in the Switzerland cohort (AUC: 0.842 to 0.762) associated with a significant distributional shift (e.g., cholesterol PSI = 11.516), attributional responses showed limited variation. A joint PSI–SHAP analysis indicates a decoupling between distributional shift and explanation behavior, with features exhibiting either high shift with stable attributions or disproportionate attributional changes. This dissociation is formalized into a three-category taxonomy: Critical, Shifted, and Stable, enabling explanation-aware auditing of model reliability. These findings suggest that attribution stability alone may be insufficient as a proxy for cross-domain robustness, underscoring the need for joint monitoring of predictive performance and explanatory validity.

title: Self-Adaptive Genetic Boosted Explainable Framework for Employee Performance Classification
venue: 2026 6th International Conference on Trends in Material Science and Inventive Materials (ICTMIM)
abstract: Accurate and interpretable employee performance evaluation is essential for effective organizational decisionmaking. This work proposes a novel explainable classification framework, termed Self-Adaptive Genetic Boosted eXplainable Framework (SAGB-XSHAP), which integrates eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGB) with a self-adaptive genetic optimization strategy and SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) - based explanation stability analysis. The proposed approach jointly evolves feature interaction structures and model hyperparameters while explicitly penalizing unstable feature attributions during optimization. Unlike conventional methods that treat interpretability as a post-processing step, the proposed framework embeds explanation consistency directly into the learning process. Experimental evaluation on a structured employee performance dataset demonstrates that the SAGBXSHAP framework accomplishes a classification accuracy of 98%, outperforming traditional Machine Learning (ML) and standard boosting-based approaches. Furthermore, SHAP-based analysis reveals consistent and meaningful influence patterns for key employee attributes such as salary, overtime, and job involvement, enabling transparent and reliable performance assessment. The results confirm that the SAGB-XSHAP framework precisely balances predictive accuracy with explanation stability, making it acceptable for practical human resource analytics implementations.

title: DualEx: Dual-Space Clustering for Regional Explanations
venue: 2025 IEEE International Conference on Data Mining Workshops (ICDMW)
abstract: Regional explanations bridge the gap between local instance-specific and global model-level explanations. However, by relying solely on the model explanation space, existing approaches may suffer from model- and explanation-specific biases. For robust explanations independent of model choices, we propose Dual-Space Regional Explanations (DualEx). DualEx takes an early-fusion, dual-space approach to form regions based on both data space (intrinsic features) and explanation space (feature attributions), weighted through a tunable parameter. We assess faithfulness of regional explanations using established clustering metrics as well as through a novel notion of cohort locality - whether explanations remain consistent and predictive within each region. In a thorough empirical evaluation study, we find that across diverse datasets, models and evaluation metrics, DualEx shows superior region quality than state-of-the-art, and provides interpretable and robust explanations that reflect data structure and model behaviour.

title: EXPLAN: Explaining Black-box Classifiers using Adaptive Neighborhood Generation
venue: 2020 International Joint Conference on Neural Networks (IJCNN)
abstract: Defining a representative locality is an urgent challenge in perturbation-based explanation methods, which influences the fidelity and soundness of explanations. We address this issue by proposing a robust and intuitive approach for EXPLaining black-box classifiers using Adaptive Neighborhood generation (EXPLAN). EXPLAN is a module-based algorithm consisted of dense data generation, representative data selection, data balancing, and rule-based interpretable model. It takes into account the adjacency information derived from the black-box decision function and the structure of the data for creating a representative neighborhood for the instance being explained. As a local model-agnostic explanation method, EXPLAN generates explanations in the form of logical rules that are highly interpretable and well-suited for qualitative analysis of the model’s behavior. We discuss fidelity-interpretability trade-offs and demonstrate the performance of the proposed algorithm by a comprehensive comparison with state-of-the-art explanation methods LIME, LORE, and Anchor. The conducted experiments on real-world data sets show our method achieves solid empirical results in terms of fidelity, precision, and stability of explanations.

title: X-DiaRisk: Explainable AI based Diabetes Risk Prediction from Clinical and Lifestyle Data
venue: 2026 International Conference on Secure Information Systems and Technologies (ICSIST)
abstract: Diabetes risk has become one of the most acute concerns in modern healthcare. The rising global prevalence of the disease increases the need for early intervention. The proposed X-DiaRisk framework is a comprehensive solution of automated risk prediction of diabetes based on systematized healthcare information. The proposed framework employs an Optuna-based CatBoost model as its baseline model along with LIME. Experimental analysis shows higher predictive performance with R2 of 0.8498, RMSE of 3.5206 and MAE of 2.8307. To increase the transparency, both LIME and SHAP are employed, providing local and global insights. The interpretability analysis revealed that family history of diabetes, physical activity, and blood pressure are the most influential predictors. A comparative evaluation between LIME and SHAP demonstrated strong agreement, with a Spearman correlation of 0.70 confirming the robustness of explanations. Thus, the proposed X-DiaRisk framework offers a practical tool for physicians, supporting efficient screening and early identification of individuals at risk of diabetes, thereby combining high predictive accuracy with explainability.

title: Cross-Domain Analysis of Fake News Detection With Explainable Transformers
abstract: The rapid dissemination of fake news across social platforms underscores the need for detection systems that are both accurate and explainable, particularly in high-stakes domains where opaque models undermine trust and accountability. This study introduces a cross-domain framework that integrates pretrained transformer models (RoBERTa, DistilBERT) with local explainable artificial intelligence techniques (SHAP, LIME) to evaluate classification performance and explanation stability jointly. Using two structurally distinct datasets, CoAID (biomedical misinformation) and PHEME (social rumors), the proposed system achieves an accuracy of up to 0.93 and F1-scores above 0.89 in cross-domain settings. Explanation consistency exceeds 0.85 under semantic and structural perturbations, revealing domain-sensitive patterns that align with linguistic and contextual cues in each corpus. Robustness analyses demonstrate resilience to noise, imbalance, and variations in virality-based thresholds. By linking prediction outcomes with token-level attribution behavior, the framework enhances interpretability without compromising performance, positioning it as a reliable approach for real-world misinformation monitoring in dynamic environments.

title: Explainable Consumer Behavior Forecasting Using Dynamic Knowledge Graphs
venue: 2026 7th International Conference On Computational Vision and Bio Inspired Computing (ICCVBIC)
abstract: The need to precisely anticipate consumer behaviour has become a prerequisite for contemporary retail, e-commerce, and customer relationship management systems, empowering companies to enhance customised advertising and marketing, demand forecasting, stock management, and customer retention. Despite the success of recent attempts to use artificial intelligence (AI) and deep learning models to improve forecast accuracy, these models remain black boxes, making them difficult to interpret, understand, and trust, and impeding their use in business decision-making. To overcome these challenges, this paper suggests a novel Dynamic Behavioural Knowledge Graph-Adaptive Causal Attention Network (DBKG-ACAN) framework for explainable consumer behaviour forecasting. In this framework, we propose fusing heterogeneous consumer data, dynamically constructing a consumer behavioural knowledge graph, applying adaptive causal attention learning, and incorporating a multi-level explainability engine and a Decision Confidence Index (DCI) into a unified framework. The Dynamic Behavioural Knowledge Graph performs continuous modelling of evolving relationships among consumers, products, transactions, and contextual factors, while the Adaptive Causal Attention Network detects behaviourally relevant interactions that directly affect the purchasing decision. The proposed framework provides global, local, causal, confidence, and recommendation-level explanations for each forecasting result and incorporates explainability into the forecasting process itself, unlike traditional explainable AI techniques that provide post hoc explanations. The proposed DBKG-ACAN approach has been successfully tested against the conventional logistic regression, random forest, support vector machine, LSTM and GNN models, yielding a forecasting accuracy of 98.14%, precision of 97.81%, recall of 97.46%, F1-score of 97.63% and AUC of 0.992, with a forecasting error of 0.041, 0.079 and 3.27% in terms of MAE, RMSE, and MAPE, respectively. Additionally, it has an Explanation Fidelity of 97.42%, Explanation Stability of 96.73%, Causal Consistency of 96.25%, Business Interpretability of 97.86%, and a Decision Confidence Index of 0.98, which shows its ability to accurately predict consumer behaviour whilst remaining transparent and trustworthy. The proposed framework can be effectively and easily implemented for intelligent retail analytics, personalised marketing, recommendation systems, and AI-supported business decision-making.

title: Explainable Machine Learning for Predicting Healthcare Workers’ Emergency Preparedness Using Disaster-Readiness and Built-Environment Indicators
abstract: Emergency preparedness among healthcare workers is commonly assessed using descriptive survey methods, which provide limited support for risk stratification, explainable decision support, and targeted institutional intervention. This study developed and internally validated an explainable machine-learning framework for predicting self-reported emergency preparedness using workforce, disaster-readiness, organizational, and perceived built-environment indicators. A cross-sectional dataset of 360 healthcare workers from 12 facilities was collected between February 10 and April 12, 2026. High self-reported preparedness was defined using a primary 70% threshold, with sensitivity analyses at 65% and 75%. Leakage-controlled models were evaluated using stratified 10-fold cross-validation, leave-one-facility-out validation, algorithm benchmarking, bootstrap confidence intervals, calibration analysis, SHAP-based explainability, SHAP stability analysis, and decision curve analysis. Adding perceived built-environment resilience to workforce, training, and emergency-exposure predictors improved ROC-AUC from 0.795 to 0.834, PR-AUC from 0.821 to 0.858, F1-score from 0.746 to 0.765, and Brier score from 0.186 to 0.167. The bootstrap mean improvement in ROC-AUC was 0.039 (95% CI, 0.016-0.065). In leave-one-facility-out validation, the final model achieved ROC-AUC 0.830 and F1-score 0.770. SHAP analysis identified previous disaster training, perceived built-environment resilience, profession, drill participation, and work area as influential predictors. Calibration was imperfect, with a slope of 0.769, indicating the need for external validation and recalibration before operational deployment. The findings show that self-reported emergency preparedness can be modeled as a multidomain health-system readiness outcome and that perceived built-environment indicators provide incremental value for explainable preparedness risk stratification.

title: Toward Explainable and Energy-Efficient Artificial Intelligence for Safety-Critical Real-World Systems
venue: 2026 6th International Conference on Electrical, Computer and Energy Technologies (ICECET)
abstract: The deployment of artificial intelligence in safety-critical real-world systems, including healthcare decision support, smart energy infrastructures, industrial monitoring, and autonomous cyber-physical systems, raises interdependent concerns about transparency, reliability, latency, and environmental sustainability. Predictive excellence alone does not guarantee operational deployability when decisions must be auditable, resource-aware, and aligned with domain risk. Although high-capacity deep learning models can achieve strong empirical performance, their opaque decision logic and computational cost limit their adoption in regulated and resource-constrained settings. This paper proposes a unified framework for explainable and energy-efficient artificial intelligence that jointly evaluates predictive utility, explanation reliability, computational efficiency, and deployment governance. The framework integrates risk-aware data profiling, transparent-first model selection, post-hoc explanation assurance, lightweight architectures, energy-aware optimization, and deployment-oriented evidence. It also defines a validation protocol that reports accuracy, robustness, latency, model size, explanation stability, and energy indicators within the same evidence scorecard. The contribution is a structured methodology for selecting AI models according to safety and sustainability constraints rather than accuracy alone. The proposed framework establishes a rigorous foundation for trustworthy and sustainable AI deployment in electrical, computer, and energy technologies.

title: Critical Analysis of Explainable AI Deficiencies and Proposal for a Causal and Adaptive Grounded Framework
venue: 2026 International Conference on Next Generation Electronics (NELEX)
abstract: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) systems are vital for reliable use in critical applications, such as fraud detection or medicine; however, popular XAI techniques like LIME and SHAP are prone to generating unreliable and causally erroneous explanations. We present in this paper ACXAI, a causality-oriented supervisory approach for XAI, combining structural causal models (SCM), stability filtering, and context-specific rules for explanation generation. We analyze the limitations of current XAI techniques along four dimensions: stability, causality, user-centricity, and deployability through formal definitions. Our empirical findings on a practical credit card fraud detection data set show that ACXAI increases the stability of the explanations (Jaccard coefficient) by up to $49 \%$, while achieving better causal consistency and without any loss in predictive accuracy compared to state-of-the-art techniques. Experimental evidence collected in healthcare and image analysis domains confirms these gains. The main contributions of our work are threefold: (1) the systematic evaluation of XAI limitations, (2) the introduction of an adaptive XAI approach based on SCM and (3) a cross-domain assessment of the proposed framework demonstrating significant improvements in terms of explanation stability and usefulness.

title: Bayesian-AIME: Quantifying Uncertainty and Enhancing Stability in Approximate Inverse Model Explanations
abstract: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), which provides the rationale behind machine learning decisions, is essential for deploying AI in high-risk domains. However, most XAI methods offer only single-point explanations that do not indicate their reliability and are often unstable. In other words, small changes in training data can lead to significantly different explanations. This study addresses these limitations by proposing a Bayesian approximate inverse model explanation method (AIME), an extension of AIME that incorporates a Bayesian framework. By modeling the inverse operator of an opaque model probabilistically, Bayesian-AIME estimates feature importance as a posterior distribution. This enables the assignment of 95% credible intervals (CIs) to feature importance scores, facilitating a quantitative assessment of explanation reliability. Using the posterior mean also improves explanation stability. The effectiveness of the method was evaluated via three experiments: 1) stability analysis via bootstrapping, 2) validation of CIs on synthetic data with known importance, and 3) case studies on Titanic survival prediction and breast cancer diagnosis. The results showed that Bayesian-AIME outperformed existing methods in terms of stability and conveyed meaningful uncertainty, thus enhancing model interpretability. This study contributes to strengthening the reliability of XAI for practical applications.

title: TAP-FL: Trust-Aware and Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning under Adversarial and Heterogeneous Settings
venue: 2026 IEEE International Conference on Industry 4.0, Artificial Intelligence, and Communications Technology (IAICT)
abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without sharing any raw data. However, real-world deployments in domains such as finance are limited by factors such as statistical heterogeneity, adversarial manipulation, privacy leakage, and low interpretability. Existing work address these challenges but are largely studied in isolation, with assessment usually limited to predictive performance. This paper proposes TAP-FL (Trust-Aware Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning), a unified federated learning framework designed to perform an extensive assessment in realistic conditions. TAP-FL uses non-IID data distributions with multiple adversarial attack settings, local differential privacy and a trust-aware aggregation mechanism which works based on update’s behavioral consistency and deviation. A multi-dimensional evaluation setup is added to collectively measure predictive performance, attack success, privacy leakage, and as well as SHAP-based analysis to measure explanation stability and attribution drift. The framework is further applied to cross-domain credit risk assessment task, combining heterogeneous models via a meta-learning formulation. Experimental results demonstrate that training stability is mostly influenced by adversarial updates, and privacy mechanisms create regulated uncertainty with minimal effect on inference risk. TAP-FL achieves consistent resilience against different types of attacks and has a consistent balance between utility and privacy, while maintaining interpretability.

title: When Accuracy Is Not Enough: Evaluating Explainable Vulnerability Detection Beyond Accuracy
abstract: Machine learning based vulnerability detection has emerged as a promising approach for improving software security at scale, particularly in domains where manual analysis is costly or impractical. Recent advances in transformer-based models, such as CodeBERT, have demonstrated strong performance on vulnerability detection benchmarks by leveraging contextual representations learned from large corpora of source code. However, the opacity of these models raises concerns about their suitability for security-critical applications, where practitioners must understand and trust model decisions. In contrast, simpler linear models using interpretable features provide transparent explanations but are often assumed to offer inferior detection performance. This paper presents a systematic comparison between an explainable baseline model based on TF-IDF character ngrams with Logistic Regression and a transformer-based model, CodeBERT, for vulnerability detection in IoT-oriented C/C++ code using the IoTvulCode dataset. In addition to standard detection metrics, we evaluate explanation faithfulness and robustness using insertion and deletion tests. Our experimental results show that although CodeBERT significantly outperforms the explainable baseline in detection accuracy, its explanations exhibit weak faithfulness under perturbation-based evaluation. Conversely, the explainable baseline produces substantially more faithful and stable explanations despite lower overall detection performance. These findings highlight a fundamental trade-off between accuracy and explanation reliability and underscore the importance of incorporating faithfulness evaluation when deploying machine learning models for vulnerability detection in security-critical environments.

title: A Multi-World Synthetic Benchmark for Evaluating RSCE in Clinical Machine Learning
abstract: Clinical machine learning (ML) models often achieve strong performance on clean test sets yet remain fragile at deployment, where measurement noise, hospital-specific distribution shift, surrogate-feature drift, label noise, and unstable explanations can lead to silent failure. Existing clinical ML benchmarks provide limited ability to probe these failure modes in a controlled, reproducible, and clinically interpretable manner. In particular, domain-style benchmarks (e.g., WILDS-like multi-environment evaluations) largely rely on pre-collected environments without mechanism-level control, while prior synthetic stress tests typically target only a narrow subset of stressors. We present a synthetic-first, perturbation-aware benchmarking framework that evaluates deployment-relevant model integrity along four complementary dimensions: Reliability ( $R$ ), Robustness under shift ( $S$ ), Calibration Stability ( $C$ ), and Explainability Stability ( $E$ ), combined into a composite RSCE index. The benchmark comprises seven analytically specified synthetic clinical “worlds” that emulate common deployment scenarios, ranging from clean in-distribution evaluation to hospital skew, measurement noise and missingness, surrogate corruption, strong nonlinearity, and label noise. These worlds are constructed via explicit perturbation operators with tunable severity ranges under a known structural data-generating process that inject controlled distortions while preserving an underlying physiological structure, enabling mechanism-isolating stress tests beyond domain labels alone. Using this testbed, we evaluate a diverse set of linear, tree-based, kernel, neural, and ensemble models across more than 15,000 model–world–perturbation configurations, and conduct external stress tests on NHANES and a MIMIC-IV hospital mortality cohort. The results reveal systematic trade-offs between discrimination, calibration, robustness, and explanation stability: models with similar AUROC on clean data can differ markedly in their behavior under realistic perturbations. Tree-based ensembles form a consistent integrity frontier, whereas several widely used models degrade sharply in calibration or attribution stability despite strong in-distribution performance. Integrity patterns learned from synthetic worlds transfer qualitatively to NHANES and MIMIC-IV, supporting RSCE as a practical pre-deployment screening and diagnostic tool. The proposed framework is fully reproducible and extensible, and is intended to serve as a synthetic-first reference benchmark for developing and vetting clinically trustworthy ML systems prior to large-scale real-world deployment.

title: PG-TabM: Domain-Informed Parameter-Efficient Ensemble Learning with Soft Physical Regularization for Concrete Compressive Strength Prediction
abstract: Accurate concrete compressive-strength prediction remains difficult when available tabular data are small, compositionally heterogeneous, and unevenly distributed across curing ages and binder systems.
